title: Technology and production methods
notes: Authored 2026-10-06 under standard v0.2.0-draft. All claims are provenance generated_gap, verification unverified.

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Describe how technology has changed and is changing production methods, and weigh its benefits and limitations.

blocks.heading: Technology in design and manufacturing
blocks.text:
Production has moved onto computers at two points. In design, computer-aided design (CAD) lets engineers draw a product on screen, test and change it - dimensions, stresses, materials - before anything physical is built, so the expensive mistakes happen on a cheap screen. In manufacturing, computer-aided manufacture (CAM) feeds those designs straight to machines that cut, weld or print to the specification, and whole lines are controlled and monitored by computer rather than by hand. Around the two sit the same pattern of change across a modern factory: stock movements tracked by barcode, quality checked by sensor, maintenance scheduled by software. A Windhoek sheet-metal shop that once cut by chalk line now cuts on a CAD-driven machine, and a Japanese car plant is the same story at a larger scale - which is why a course written for Namibian factories still teaches CAD and CAM by name.

Weighed: the benefits are higher productivity and consistent quality, less waste of material and time, and machines that run without fatigue; the limitations are heavy investment, the cost and time of training, maintenance and breakdown risk, and work that disappears when a line is automated. The technology spreads where its savings outweigh those costs - and rarely without the retraining.

blocks.heading: Worked contrast: the same panel, before and after
blocks.text: Before: a Windhoek shop cuts a door panel by hand from a chalk line. The cut takes 40 minutes, and the tenth panel differs slightly from the first because the hand that guides the blade tires. After: the panel is drawn once in CAD, tested for fit on screen, and cut by a CAM-driven machine in 6 minutes - and the thousandth panel matches the first, because the specification is carried by the machine. That is the change in one example: the design decisions moved upstream onto the screen, and the consistency moved into the machine, which is why the spread of CAD and CAM continues even where the investment is painful.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Automation is one of the two named routes to productivity in 4.1.1; its costs and scale requirements meet the break-even and economies-of-scale analysis of 4.2, its quality consistency is judged in 4.3, and the workers it displaces are the human-resource concerns of 2.2.
